svg.title: Quarkus: I/O threads vs worker threads
svg.desc: Two requests wait on the same database for the same time. Request A calls an endpoint that returns Uni, so it runs on the event-loop thread, and that thread stays free while the database works. Request B calls an endpoint that returns a plain object, so the event loop hands it to a worker thread, which stays parked for its whole JDBC call. A timeline shows what each thread does, including what happens when the same JDBC call blocks the event loop, and a table compares the two kinds of thread.
svg.text: Quarkus: I/O threads vs worker threads
Every request arrives on an I/O (event-loop) thread. The endpoint's return type decides whether your code runs there or on a worker.
non-blocking call: the I/O thread moves on
1 of N event loops (N = CPU cores)

g.text: A calls availableSeats(), which returns Uni<…>, so Quarkus runs it on the I/O thread.
B calls salesReport(), which returns a plain object, so the I/O thread hands it to a worker.
Both now wait on PostgreSQL. A's query holds no thread; B's JDBC call parks executor-thread-1.
While both wait, the I/O thread is free and keeps serving other requests.
A's rows arrive. Its continuation runs on the same event loop, which writes the response.
B's JDBC call returns. The worker finishes salesReport(); the I/O thread writes the bytes.
Same database latency for A and B. A's wait held no thread; B's wait held a worker the whole time.

svg.text: Anti-pattern: the same JDBC call made on the I/O thread (for example, blocking code inside a method that returns Uni)

g.text: B's JDBC call blocks the whole loop
C, D, E, A delayed up to 3 s
Vert.x logs a blocked-thread warning after 2 s
